headline: Trump, Xi and Putin issue a "peace declaration" as Iran claims an attack in Kuwait
standfirst: Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen on Thursday promising talks on nuclear risks, but saying nothing about Ukraine or Iran. Iran says it targeted a base in Kuwait, Russian strikes killed four in Odesa, and COP31 is stuck on fossil fuels.

essentials.title: In Shenzhen, Trump, Xi and Putin issue a "peace declaration" silent on Ukraine and Iran
essentials.standfirst: Meeting as a trio for the first time, on the sidelines of APEC, the American, Chinese and Russian leaders issued a text promising dialogue on nuclear risks. The declaration mentions neither the war in Ukraine nor the war with Iran.
body: Meeting in Shenzhen on Thursday November 19th, on the sidelines of the APEC summit, for a first three-way session of more than an hour chaired by Xi Jinping, the Chinese, American and Russian leaders issued a "peace declaration" reaffirming that a nuclear war cannot be won, according to Reuters.

The largely symbolic text, as the agency describes it, sets out an open-ended dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing proliferation, pledges UN reform, more fuel supplies and respect for the immunity of leaders before international courts, but mentions neither the war in Ukraine nor the one with Iran.

Vladimir Putin conceded that the declaration set no ambitious goals and said he would consider attending the G20 that Donald Trump hosts in Florida next month, while Ukraine's foreign minister, Andriy Sybiha, said Shenzhen had not turned out to be the "Yalta" Moscow had dreamed of.

figure.label: leading nuclear powers gathered around one table
figure.compare: with no commitment to cut arsenals in the declaration, according to Reuters

positions.wants: Donald Trump says Xi Jinping agreed that the Strait of Hormuz must stay open and that Iran must not have a nuclear weapon.
Xi Jinping urges the powers to shed a "Cold War mentality" and repeats that a nuclear war must never be fought.

next.t: G20 summit in Florida, where Donald Trump is due to meet Xi Jinping again.

items.name: Shenzhen
items.note: Host city of the APEC summit, where Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin held their first three-way meeting on Thursday.

analysis.title: A summit of modest ambitions
analysis.text: The declaration shows how far apart the three remain: since New START expired, Washington has wanted to bring Beijing into arms control, but China refuses to negotiate over its smaller arsenal, and the text contains no commitment to cuts, according to Reuters. The pledge to respect leaders' immunity before international courts comes more than three years after the International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Vladimir Putin, whose government rejects the allegations. Trade remains unresolved: the truce struck in Busan in October 2025, after an escalation that had pushed American tariffs on Chinese goods as high as 145%, has been extended to January 10th 2027, according to Al Jazeera, and Donald Trump is due to see Xi Jinping again at the G20 in Florida.

keys.title: The fuel pledge
keys.text: The three powers promise to increase supplies of fuel products for all countries, according to Reuters, as the war with Iran disrupts the Gulf. Al Jazeera notes that it is unclear how the pledge will be put into practice.

keys.title: The Beijing-Moscow axis
keys.text: Xi Jinping described Sino-Russian relations as solid "as a mountain". The two leaders signed more than 40 co-operation agreements at a summit in Beijing in May.

keys.title: Ukraine on the sidelines
keys.text: Absent from the declaration, the war in Ukraine dominated the bilateral talks between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, according to Al Jazeera. The same day, European and Ukrainian leaders were due to meet the American envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Berlin.

essentials.title: Iran claims an attack on a base in Kuwait as ships are hit near Hormuz
essentials.standfirst: Iran's army says it targeted the Ali Al Salem base in Kuwait on Wednesday in retaliation for the American strike on Qeshm. A vessel belonging to the Emirati firm Adnoc was attacked off Oman, leaving 11 injured and one missing.
body: Iran's army said on Wednesday November 18th that its drones had targeted Patriot air-defence batteries at the Ali Al Salem base in Kuwait, which hosts American forces, in retaliation for Washington's strike the day before on a missile site on Qeshm island, according to Press TV, quoted by ABC News.

Washington has not confirmed the claims; meanwhile Iran's navy says three tankers caught fire after hitting mines east of the Strait of Hormuz, and Adnoc's shipping arm reports 11 injured and one missing aboard one of its vessels, attacked off Oman on Tuesday night.

The head of Iran's army, General Amir Hatami, promises a response "without geographical limits" to any further American action, while Riyadh and Abu Dhabi have condemned the attacks and Bahrain is calling for action by the Security Council, on the eve of the Shenzhen summit.

analysis.title: Hormuz, a maritime battlefield
analysis.text: Since April the United States has enforced a naval blockade of Iran's ports on the Gulf and the Gulf of Oman, now backed by three aircraft carriers after the Theodore Roosevelt joined the George H.W. Bush and the George Washington, according to Gulf News. Tehran has responded by claiming attacks on shipping and often blaming the damage on mines. The speaker of Iran's parliament and chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, has warned that any dam, port or power station near an American or Israeli base could be treated as a dual-use target. Diplomatically, the memorandum of understanding signed in June to end the war remains a dead letter, according to ABC News, and Pakistan is awaiting Washington's reply to an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait.

keys.title: Economic pressure
keys.text: America's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, expects Iran's economy to shrink by 25% over the coming year. A new force, dubbed "Iron Gate", is targeting Iran's overland and Caspian routes, according to Gulf News.

keys.title: The Yemeni front
keys.text: The Saudi-led coalition says it struck 60 Houthi targets on Tuesday and intercepted two cruise missiles fired towards Riyadh on Wednesday. The Houthis claim to have targeted oil pumping stations.

keys.title: The airlines
keys.text: Etihad has suspended flights between Abu Dhabi, Riyadh and Dammam until Thursday. The Emirates is keeping its ban on citizens travelling to Iran.

essentials.title: Russian strikes kill four in Odesa as Brussels offers Kyiv a €45bn loan
essentials.standfirst: Russian strikes hit Odesa's historic centre, part of it a UNESCO World Heritage site, on Wednesday, killing at least four people. The European Commission is proposing a €45bn loan for next year.
body: At least four people were killed and 13 injured in Odesa on Wednesday November 18th when three Russian strikes hit the historic centre, including a UNESCO-protected area, according to local officials, with Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of striking again after rescuers arrived.

The same day the European Commission proposed a €45bn loan to cover part of a financing gap put at €70bn for next year, to be repaid only once Russia has paid reparations, according to its president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Overnight Ukrainian forces struck the Crimean bridge again, where rail traffic was suspended according to Russia's transport ministry, while the coalition of the willing meets in Berlin on Thursday to discuss air defence and energy.

analysis.title: An energy war on both sides
analysis.text: According to Ukraine's energy ministry, Russia has carried out more than 1,000 attacks on energy infrastructure since September, and the situation remains "extremely difficult" in the Dnipropetrovsk and Kharkiv regions, where repeated strikes are hampering repairs. Ukraine is hitting back at Russian refining: according to Reuters, cited by the Kyiv Independent, its attacks disrupted or halted 15 of the country's 35 big refineries in 20 days, cutting processing capacity by 45%. The strategy divides Kyiv's allies: Germany's defence minister, Boris Pistorius, called "stupid" the criticism of Ukraine's long-range strikes by a senior Pentagon official, Elbridge Colby. Talks, meanwhile, continue after the meeting in Abu Dhabi, where a prisoner exchange was agreed.

keys.title: The European loan
keys.text: The budget support proposed by the Commission is conditional on reforms, notably on the rule of law and fighting corruption. It still needs the approval of the European Parliament and the Council.

keys.title: The Berlin meeting
keys.text: Volodymyr Zelensky set out the agenda for the coalition of the willing, focused on air defence and energy support. American envoys are also due to meet Ukrainian officials there, according to Al Jazeera.

keys.title: The Crimean bridge
keys.text: A section of the bridge collapsed after a first Ukrainian strike on Tuesday, which killed two people according to Al Jazeera. Rail traffic had resumed before the new attack.

essentials.title: At COP31 in Antalya, phasing out fossil fuels divides delegates two days before the close
essentials.standfirst: The draft deal published on Monday offers two options on fossil fuels, one of them an outright phase-out. The European Union wants major changes, and the conference is due to end on Friday.
body: Some 200 countries gathered in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31 are haggling over an 18-page draft decision published on Monday November 16th, which offers two options on fossil fuels: the transition away from them agreed in 2023, or an outright phase-out.

The EU's climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra, says the text needs a thorough overhaul, while dozens of European, African and Pacific states that want the next IPCC report before COP33 are up against a bloc that includes Saudi Arabia and India.

Australia's minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations under a presidency shared with Turkey, admitted that some clauses had already been rejected and promised at least one new draft before the close, due on Friday November 20th, though COPs often overrun.

positions.wants: A substantially amended draft decision, without which the talks could become untenable, according to Wopke Hoekstra.

next.t: Scheduled close of COP31 in Antalya.

analysis.title: The old fossil-fuel divide
analysis.text: The text repeats the 2023 pledge to transition away from fossil fuels, but also offers more ambitious wording that oil producers have fought for years; according to Reuters, both could vanish from the final deal. The draft also calls on rich countries to reach net zero as early as 2030, a prospect that Antigua and Barbuda's environment minister, Michael Joseph, thinks will be very hard to sell. Other issues divide delegates: adaptation finance for poor countries and a Turkish proposal to raise electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035. Every decision requires consensus, which is why conferences often run on for days, while a UN report published last month found the world on course to overshoot 1.5°C of warming.

keys.title: The shared presidency
keys.text: Turkey is hosting the conference, chaired by its minister Murat Kurum, while Australia, represented by Chris Bowen, leads the negotiations. Such a division of roles is unprecedented in the history of COPs.

keys.title: The IPCC report
keys.text: The panel of experts suspended its last meeting, and a new session is planned for December. The timetable for its seventh assessment report has become one of the sticking points of the conference.

keys.title: The AI pledge
keys.text: Only nine of the roughly 200 countries present had signed Turkey's proposed pledge on artificial intelligence early in the week, according to Reuters.

essentials.title: On the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, the two armies mass around Badme
essentials.standfirst: According to conflict monitors and sources close to Tigrayan militias, Addis Ababa and Asmara have concentrated forces along their border. Fire has been exchanged near Badme, the flashpoint of the 1998-2000 war.
body: Ethiopia and Eritrea have massed forces along their shared border, according to the conflict monitor ACLED, the International Crisis Group and two sources close to Tigrayan militias quoted by Reuters on Wednesday November 18th, raising fears of open war between the neighbours.

According to ACLED, Ethiopian drones struck probable Eritrean positions around Badme on November 12th, Eritrea answered with artillery and the two armies clashed on the Ethiopian side the next day, the first direct exchanges in more than a month, which Reuters could not confirm.

Eritrea's information minister, Yemane Gebremeskel, decries "propaganda" from Addis Ababa's ruling party, which has not responded, while Magnus Taylor, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, fears that fighting against Tigrayan rebels could drag the two countries into direct conflict.

analysis.title: Yesterday's allies, rivals once more
analysis.text: Reconciled by their 2018 peace deal, Ethiopia and Eritrea fought side by side in the Tigray war of 2020-22. Relations then soured, not least after Ethiopia's prime minister, Abiy Ahmed, called for his country to regain access to the sea, which Asmara read as an implicit threat of aggression, though Addis Ababa insists it wants to achieve this peacefully. The fighting between the federal army and Tigrayan rebels since September has brought the danger closer to the border, especially as Ethiopia's army is pursuing the rebels to its edge. Eritrea, independent since 1993, accuses its neighbour of seeking a pretext to invade. Badme, whose control sparked the 1998-2000 war, was awarded to Eritrea by a boundary commission after the conflict.

keys.title: The 1998-2000 war
keys.text: The border conflict between the two countries killed tens of thousands of people. The town of Badme was its main prize.

keys.title: Access to the sea
keys.text: Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Abiy Ahmed's remarks on the subject feed Asmara's mistrust.

keys.title: Outside backers
keys.text: Addis Ababa accuses Sudan, itself in the grip of civil war, and Egypt of backing the Tigrayan rebels. Eritrea, Sudan and Egypt all deny it.
